For this year’s race, the Post will send one question to candidates running for City Council every week until election day. The School Board election was cancelled due to a lack of candidates to challenge the incumbents. This week, only City Council candidates were sent a question. The five city council candidates vying for three open seats were sent the question on Monday, August 24, and were asked to reply with a 200-word response. Week 1 Question: Who are you, why are you running, and name one thing you have worked on in Piedmont that voters can look up? Tom Ramsey Incumbent My wife and I drove from the Midwest to California in an old Volkswagen bus on our honeymoon. Luckily, that thing made it to the Bay Area, and eventually we moved to Piedmont in 1997, where we raised our two daughters. Professionally, I’ve been a licensed California architect since 1990, and now I work for a national real estate advisory firm. I am running for re-election because experienced leadership makes a difference. My focus remains on rigorous fiscal oversight, maintaining balanced budgets, and prioritizing public safety. I am committed to smart planning—navigating state housing mandates while preserving Piedmont’s historic charm. During my seven years on the Planning Commission, I worked with the team that completed a comprehensive update to our city’s Design Guidelines. That document is actively shaping how we preserve our neighborhood integrity today. On the City Council, we updated those guidelines to stay ahead of state mandates and code changes, providing design guardrails to manage growth responsibly. Since you elected me to the City Council in November 2022, it has been an honor to work alongside you to keep Piedmont safe, vibrant, and connected. I would be grateful for your vote to continue serving our community.

articles.text: The Beach School Dads Club hosted its 21st annual Pancake Breakfast on Sunday, August 30 in grand proportion and style. Moore serenaded the crowd on saxophone while walking among the revelers. He created his own lyrics about endless pancakes and the carnival-like atmosphere of the event. articles.text: Four more years for Thomasson and Medhekar Veteran school board members Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar are running unopposed in the November 3 General Election as incumbent candidates. articles.text: Organizers of the annual Adult Recreation Expo are seeking local organizations that offer recreational, educational, or social programs and activities for adults to showcase their offerings at Piedmont’s third annual Adult Recreation Expo. The Expo will take place on Sunday, November 15 from 2-4:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building. Exhibiting at the Expo is a great way to reach new audiences - the event attracted over 200 attendees in each of its first two years. Sign up by September 14 to guarantee your spot. Groups interested in exhibiting should email lgardner555@gmail.com and campktgrp@comcast.net to sign up: There is no cost to participate. • Expo organizers will provide a table and chairs. Exhibitors will be responsible for providing displays or materials to distribute. An attendee going through a rowing machine demonstration. Attendees of the Adult Recreation Expo browse comics and sketchbooks. • • Exhibitors should plan to have two representatives present at their table for the full event. Organizers request that exhibitors announce the event to their members. The Expo, anchored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, Piedmont Adult School, and Piedmont Center for the Arts and organized by volunteers. Now in its third year, the Expo grew from the work of a Recreation Commission subcommittee on older adult programming. After reviewing existing activities throughout Piedmont, as well as nearly 500 responses to a community survey, the subcommittee identified a lack of knowledge about existing opportunities as a primary barrier to connecting adults with the activities they were interested in. The Expo aims to bridge this gap. The Adult Recreation Expo is organized by volunteers Dick Carter, former Recreation Commission Chair, and current commission member Lisa Gardner. For more information, visit piedmont.ca.gov/AdultExpo. Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at ­ Mulberry’s Market. This clever, enthusiastic huntress loves leaping after toys, and her stealthy ambushes are adorably serious. After playtime, she’s happy to take a catnap, or follow the people in her life from room to room like a faithful sidekick. Pepita plays hard and feels her feelings deeply. She can get startled and overwhelmed easily. While daily anxiety medication helps her stay relaxed (and is easily mixed into her meals) she will also rely on her adopter to read her body language and guide her back to a calm state. This affectionate, curious Adopt Pepita through Cat Town. girl is looking for a quiet, adult-only home where she can be the one and only cat — and a person who will appreciate everything that makes her unmistakably Pepita. articles.text: In a planned turf replacement, the company FieldTurf, located in Montreal, arrived at Hampton Park and began removing the existing well-worn artificial turf on Monday, August 24, on the first phase of replacing the field. The field will be closed to the public throughout the duration of the project, which is estimated to take three weeks. The rest of the park will remain open. The City’s artificial fields are serviced twice a year through a contract with FieldTurf’s maintenance staff. During their most recent visit, the turf maintenance staff reported substantial tears in the path between second and third bases. There is concern for the players’ safety if the field is not replaced. FieldTurf noted that the quality of the turf blades has degenerated to the point that it’s challenging for the turf to hold the sand and cork infill. Artificial turf has an approximate life expectancy of 8-10 years. Hampton Field’s turf field was installed in 2016, marking 10 years with the turf in place. The field’s new design has been coordinated with the consultant Lloyd Engineering to ensure the changes meet the Recreation Department’s needs. “We understand the bases are high-wear zones; those areas have been designed so that if, in 2-3 years, they need to be replaced, the carpet can be cut, removed, and replaced in a less than awkward scenario,” said Park Director Nancy Kent. FieldTurf provided the turf for Witter Field and the Linda Beach Field and will be replacing the Hampton Field turf. The contract was awarded to the company for $171,824. articles.text: Chief Teaching & Learning Officer, Exploratorium A few weeks into the new school year, families are settling into familiar rhythms. We’re hearing from teachers, adjusting to new schedules, and getting a sense for what kids will be learning this year. We might be feeling excited, nervous, or a little of both. It can be daunting to know the best way to support kids and teens as they head back to school. As they get older, we may have less visibility into the classroom, less familiarity with the content they’re learning, or hear less directly from them. But what if a new school year was also an invitation for us, as parents and caregivers, to become learners again? Imagine a young child asks you why the sky is blue. You might already know something about how gases in the air scatter sunlight, or you might quickly look it up on your phone. But consider what happens when you instead say, “I’m not sure. What do you think?” That simple, curious response can open a completely different conversation. Instead of moving quickly from question to answer, we can linger in the space between. We can make a guess, look more closely, test an idea, change our minds, and figure something out together. Meeting questions with curiosity and an intention to understand is a form of inquiry-based learning, and it doesn’t require a science lab or a lesson plan. It can happen when a child wonders why the moon is visible during the day, why some songs get stuck in their head, or how an algorithm decides what they see online. Ask another question. Make a prediction. Look for evidence together. Let one question lead to another. Older kids may be less likely to wonder aloud, but they still have BIG questions about themselves, others, and the world around them. Create space to hear what’s on their minds, and meet their questions with that same spirit of curiosity. Invite them into your questions, too, even if the immediate response is an eye roll! At the Exploratorium, this kind of curiosity-driven, inquiry-based learning is at the center of everything we do. This summer, my team welcomed dozens of teachers from across California to spend several weeks learning and experimenting with us. We work with educators in all 58 California counties, giving them opportunities to step out of their role as experts and become learners again. They investigate things, follow their own questions, try ideas that don’t work, and bring that spirit of inquiry back to their classrooms. We like to imagine a world in which all adults are lifelong learners. Our kids are growing up with instant access to the most expansive set of information in history. Classrooms, technology, and education are – and should be – changing because of this. Curiosity, creativity, and connection remain essential. It will be the humans in the next generation who keep asking questions who will lead us forward. So this school year, support the kids in your life to be inquisitive by showing them what that looks like. Let them hear you say, “I’ve never thought about that before.” Wonder out loud. Be willing to try something and get it wrong. Our kids have plenty to learn this year. So do we. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life. A family gets up close and curious at the Exploratorium’s Skin Scope exhibit.
articles.title: Back to school, back to inquiry

articles.text: The Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center’s fall fundraising campaign is off to a strong start thanks to a generous $30,000 gift from Dress Best for Less (DBFL). “The emotional well-being of teenagers plays a key role in their success and happiness, and DBFL is proud to support the Wellness Center in achieving this goal,” said DBFL President Nagisa Yamamoto. The donation will fully offset the cost of a Wellness Center counselor, helping keep mental health and wellness services free and accessible to Piedmont students. The gift will enable the Wellness Center to support the stipend for a counseling intern for the 2026-2027 school year. Partners like DBFL are essential to the long-term viability of the Wellness Center. Founded in 1982 to support Piedmont schools, the non-profit DBFL retail store accepts and resells new or gently used items, donating profits to the community while supporting sustainability efforts by keeping clothing and household goods out of landfill. Community members can support DBFL’s work by shopping at the retail store on Piedmont Avenue or volunteering. The PUSD Wellness Center serves students at Piedmont High School, Middle School and Millennium High School. Counselors provide free, confidential counseling on campus and connect students and families with community resources. Students can seek scheduled or drop-in support for challenges including academic stress, anxiety, depression, grief, relationship conflicts and substance use concerns. During the 2025-26 school year, Wellness Center counselors provided over 1,620 therapy sessions to students while another 100 students received ongoing, individualized support. The Center also offers students healthy PUSD Wellness Center staff stand in front of the new Gratitude Wall recognizing donors. Front row: Sabine Scott (left), Makeda Mayes, Nemo Baker, and Tyler Hill. Back row: Min Chen-Gaddini (left), İlke Bayazitli, Maddy Sage, Sari Sanghvi, and Carol Menz. snacks and health resources on a drop-in basis, another way it creates a welcoming space. This year, the Wellness Center Support Committee must raise an additional $50,000 to ensure that the Wellness Center can continue offering the same level of support to Piedmont’s students. Donors of $500 or more will receive an invitation for two to a sponsor reception at a private home in Piedmont. Those who contribute $1,000 or more will also have their names added to the Gratitude Wall outside the Wellness Center at Piedmont High School, an artist-designed installation of translucent tiles, each featuring the name of a generous donor who has helped support the Wellness Center. Inaugurated in May of 2026 and rotated annually, the wall recognizes the families and community members whose generosity helps support counseling hours and a safe space for Piedmont students. Contributions help fund counseling staff stipends, program supplies and student support activities. This year’s fundraising campaign, which launched August 12, will help the Center continue offering its current range of programs and services. To contribute to the 2026 campaign or learn more, visit Piedmontwellness.org To learn more about shopping, donating or volunteering with DBFL, visit dressbestforless.org

articles.text: Tally Ho! Books is hosting an author event on Thursday, September 10 with Piedmont resident and law professor David Oppenheimer in conversation with Lois Corrin. The event will be a discussion of Oppenheimer's newest book The Diversity Principle, which traces the deep history of diversity as a principle of equality, learning, and democracy. The event will take place at Tally Ho! Books, 3941 Piedmont Ave., at 7 p.m. Oppenheimer is a Clinical Professor of Law at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, where he teaches Civil Procedure and Evidence Law and serves as Co-Director of the Berkeley Center on Comparative Equality and Anti-Discrimination Law and of the law school’s pro bono program. He is the author or editor of 10 books and scores of articles on US and global discrimination law. Throughout his career, Oppenheimer has worked to understand and address systemic inequality and discrimination from a legal perspective and to make this knowledge accessible to a His new book challenges the conventional wisdom about the origins of the modern idea of diversity. In popular understanding, diversity is usually traced to the American civil rights movement. The Diversity Principle reveals a forgotten history – that diversity was embraced as an effort to improve knowledge and judgment more than a century David Oppenheimer will appear at Tally Ho! Books on Thursday, September 10, to discuss his newest book The Diversity Principle. before it became a principle of equality. articles.text: 30+ Kidlit Creators join this year’s event More than 30 of the Bay Area’s kidlit (children’s literature) creators will fill Children’s Fairyland with storytelling magic on Saturday, September 19 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The park celebrates books, book lovers, and the people who bring books to life. Librarian and host of Reading Rainbow, Mychal Threets, and this year’s Caldecott Medal winner, Cátia Chien, bring the annual Children’s Book Festival into a class of its own. The festival brings together young readers, writers, and artists for a joyful day of storytelling, meet-and-greets, book signings, and interactive programming, all included with general admission. Speakers at the 2026 Children’s Book Festival: • Cátia Chien, illustrator, 2026 Caldecott Medal Winner and a Golden Kite Award winner. • Joanna Ho, author, recipient of the Asian/Pacific American Award for Children’s Literature Honor, a Golden Kite Award, and more. • Cindy Derby, illustrator, and recipient of a 2021 Caldecott Honor and Golden Kite Award. • Randy Ribay, author, co-winner of the Michael L. Printz Award and winner of the Asian Pacific American Library Association Medal. • Mychal Threets, beloved librarian, author, mental health activist/advocate, and host of revived children’s TV show Reading Rainbow. • Youth Writers Workshop led by author Natasha Tripplett. Guests will have the opportunity to participate in hands-on An attendee finishes a comic book strip at cartoonist Jen De Oliveira’s table at 2024’s Children’s Book Festival. activities hosted by the Oakland Public Library. The festival also spotlights Fairyland’s Youth Writers’ Workshop, where young authors (ages 8–12) will share their original stories in an anthology, presenting alongside their mentor, local author and educator, Natasha Tripplett. Independent local bookseller Books on B will be on site for guests to browse and purchase books. “Books are just the beginning,” said Vicky Chen, senior director of education and community. “Books open the door to creativity, empathy, connection, belonging, and so much more. We’re thrilled to celebrate the stories that bring us together, build bridges across communities, and spark the imagination of every child who walks through our Fairy Gates.” Throughout the park, families can meet authors and illustrators, hear stories read aloud by the creators themselves, watch illustration demos, and shop for books from the Books on B pop-up shop. The event will be emceed by beloved educator Peter Limata, host of “Storytime with Mr. Limata.” Additional community programming includes hands-on activities from local literacy partners, art-making stations, and family literacy resources. “There’s nothing quite like watching a child fall in love with books,” said Angela Moffett, Fairyland’s librarian and a member of the Caldecott Award Selection Committee. “The Children’s Book Festival gives young readers a chance to meet the people behind the pages, discover new favorites, and feel the joy of being a part of a community that values literacy and the art of storytelling. For children who love books, and all lovers of children’s literature, the book festival at Fairyland is truly the best day of the year.” Tickets and more information are available on Fairyland’s website: https://fairyland.org/ book-festival/.

articles.text: On Wednesday, August 26, a coalition of states reached a $17 billion settlement with Meta in a Child Safety Trial. The states of California, New Jersey, Kentucky, and Colorado alleged the tech giant designed its apps (Instagram and Facebook) to be addictive to kids and knew about the risks those platforms posed, but hid that information from the public. The states accused Meta of designing algorithms that encourage compulsive use with features such as infinite scroll, photo filters, and the “like” button. The states claim the company knew the platforms were addictive to kids, but publicly downplayed the risks. The states also accuse Meta of violating the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, by collecting data from users under 13 without parental consent. According to the State of California Department of Justice, the settlement requires Meta to pay up to $17 billion in penalties to the states over 10 years and to make significant changes to how its platforms operate to make them safer for minors. If approved by a judge, a few of these changes would include: • A default daily time limit of two hours for users under 18, which can only be lifted by a parent. • An enhanced mechanism for teens to report potentially harmful content and a requirement that Meta respond to 90% of those reports within six hours. • A ban on displaying likes or reactions to users under 18. • An option for users under 18 to have a non-personalized feed, meaning a feed that doesn’t use an algorithm to target them with content aimed to keep them endlessly scrolling. • A commitment from Meta to maintain, review, and improve existing teen content safety measures. California will receive up to $2.1 billion if the settlement is approved, according to a statement from Attorney General Rob Bonta. Meta will set aside some of the settlement money to address mental health harm to kids, while the California Legislature and governor will decide how to spend a portion. “We have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of difference for children and their families,” said Bonta. The Post spoke with two high school students to understand their feelings about being directly targeted by social media companies. “It’s honestly not surprising hearing about the Meta safety violations,” said PHS student Julia Stokes. “The effect of social media is definitely noticeable in our generation; it’s become integrated into every aspect of our lives.” “It feels terrifying in a sense to know they are trying to look me up in the media, and it was created specifically for my generation. I feel manipulated and scared for what else these large companies can do with mass amounts of power,” added PHS student Ayla Blanford. Both said they would like to see the government target other social media companies that are likely committing the same acts as Meta, but quieter. They hope that the federal government provides further restrictions on social media to protect the younger generation as they enter the online space earlier and earlier in their lives.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont got its first win of the season in a 7-0 victory over University. Piedmont High’s flag football team captured its first win of the season on Tuesday, August 25 when visiting University in San Francisco. It was a defensive 7-0 victory. They followed up two days later with a 41-0 loss at Witter Field to Las Lomas, which was last year’s No. 1 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section bracket. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 1-3 to start its season. Of the four games, three of their opponents featured in last year’s NCS postseason, including Acalanes reaching the D2 championship and Las Lomas being D1 semifinalists as the top seed. “We’re learning that we can catch it and go long. We know there are better possibilities in the future,” said coach Beth Black. Against University, Piedmont got it done with defense. Their game-winning score came early in the fourth quarter when Nea Mafi intercepted a pass near the Red Devils’ end zone. It led to quarterback Ellie Elmquist hitting Agatha Filha-Gama for a short-yardage touchdown. Four games into the season Black has her eyes on Cea’naiya Alexander, who had an interception and 62 receiving yards against Las Lomas. “Naiya was phenomenal on all sides. If that grows with the other players, then the network continues. She’s bringing everything she has to practice and to the game, our goal was to connect with her on long passes. One of the big things to sharpen up overall is the energy level and to get a message across that they are just as fast as the girls on Las Lomas. We have to show that speed,” Black said. PHS now looks ahead to the start of its Western Alameda County Conference schedule, while also hosting the first “Battle of the Bay” Highlander Showcase on Saturday, September 5. Four games will be played at Witter Field when one East Bay team will face off against a school from San Francisco. Piedmont faces St. Ignatius at 10:30 a.m. and Oakland Tech plays George Washington of SF at 9:00 a.m., Bishop O’Dowd plays University at 12:00 p.m., and Berkeley plays Lowell at 1:30 p.m. 7-0 over University Piedmont got its touchdown when Mafi intercepted a pass near University’s goal line in the early minutes of the fourth quarter. Down around the one, Ellie Elmquist found Filha-Gama for a short-yardage touchdown reception. It was the team’s first offensive touchdown of the season. Final stats: Elmquist had 56 passing yards, 63 rushing yards, and one touchdown pass. Alexander had one reception for eight yards and 12 rushing yards. Mafi had 59 rushing yards, three tackles, one sack, one interception, and three pass defenses. Skye Prata-Baack had four receptions for 36 yards, and one tackle. Zayda Weber had one reception for five yards. Maddie Lee had seven tackles and two sacks. Cory Minor had 12 tackles, Kate Tong had six, Bea Nackley had five, Sophia Puckett had four, and Carmela Dilauro had three. Cea’naiya Alexander reels in a long pass against Las Lomas. She also had an interception.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross-country team returns to toe the line on Saturday, September 5 at the St. Mary’s Invitational at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. The girls team is back after reaching last year’s Division 4 CIF State Championship, placing 18th of 25 teams. It marked the first time the school has sent a full girls squad since 2019. Only two members of last year’s girls team departed with the Class of 2026, Skylar Best and Cora Chun. The squad is set to bring back several key runners: Leighton Mand, Viviane Oesterer, Amalia Gray, Cora Brozowski-Schrader, Nikita Gorelik, and Kelsey Coleman – providing the Highlanders a solid group of returning runners. Camille Hauser and Madeleine Ewen are also making their mark. “They should be a strong team, but the caveat is always everyone staying injury free,” said coach Dresden Schulte-Sasse (right) is emerging as a leader for the boys’ cross country team. Cora Brozowski-Schrader has been named a captain for the girls’ cross country team. Photos by Jenni Tsoi-Best Leighton Mand returns as a four-year starter. She was Piedmont’s leadrunner at the 2025 D4 CIF State Championship. Steve Zirkelbach. “The team is led by Leighton, Amalia, and Cora, with Nikita, Viviane, and Kelsey also returning. Camille Hauser and Madeleine Ewen also round out our top-eight and we’re very excited about them.” Mand is a four-year varsity starter. She was the Post’s 2025 Sophomore of the Year and our honorable mention for 2024 Freshman of the Year. She was the lead runner at State for Piedmont, finishing 96th of 205 runners with a time of 19:52.3 on the 5,000 meter course. She was a key runner throughout last year’s campaign and earned the Post’s Athlete of the Month in September, October, and November. She battled an injury during the spring track season but looks to be recovered to start the fall. “She and Amalia had some recurring pain in her feet, so we continue to monitor those. They are getting close to 100 percent, it’s coming around and we’ll have to see what happens this weekend to determine where everyone is,” Zirkelbach said. Zirkelbach also named Brozowski-Schrader a team captain. Coleman burst onto the scene as a freshman in 2025. “Cora has looked strong, she’s looking really good in training. She’s a captain with Leighton. Kelsey is back with us and she is right up there in our top-seven. It’s hard to determine just how everything will shake out; it’s a close group,” Zirkelbach said. The boys’ team will have to compete without senior Sebastien Swain who suffered a broken toe. One runner who is looking ahead for a big season is junior Dresden Schulte-Sasse, who reached the track NCS Bayshore Area Championship last spring in the 1600 and 3200. “Seb unfortunately had an accident and broke a toe this summer. Dresden is looking like possibly our strongest runner. He’s looking really good. He got a lot stronger over the summer and is very interested in trying to be at the top of the heap,” Zirkelbach said. Other returning runners include junior Aaron Bennett and senior Alex Schleuning. Both reached the NCS Bayshore 3200 in track. Schulte-Sasse was 14th of 24, and Schleuning was 19th, and Bennett 20th. “We’re looking to Aaron and Alex,” Zirkelbach said. “Aaron is looking strong; he’s very focused and is very committed. We had a 3200 time trial, and Dresden came out on top with Alex and Aaron behind him.” Also emerging for the boys are Dylan Wallway, Luca LaForte, and Jack Shim as the team’s possible best-six. “We have Dylan returning as a sophomore and Luca LaForte will be emerging this season. Jack Shim is looking pretty strong and I’m excited to see what he can do,” Zirkelbach said.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team got its season started in impressive fashion with a pair of victories on back-to-back days. They hosted Acalanes to a 7-0 sweep on Wednesday, August 26 and followed up with a close 4-3 win over Marin Catholic the next day. “The season has begun and we are off to a good start. After playing two scrimmages last week, we were warmed up and won both our matches,” coach Jim Landes said. It was a terrific week for No. 1 singles starter, sophomore Ella Ruthven, who beat two opponents to whom she lost last year. Ruthven was the Post’s honorable mention for our 2026 Freshman of the Year award. Ruthven won in three-sets over Acalanes’ Elisabetta Sokolova, 6-1, 5-7, 11-9, and also beat Marin Catholic’s Christiane Zuber in straight sets, 6-2, 6-1. “In the second set [against Sokolova], I lost some of my consistency and she started making more of her forehand. When it came to the tiebreak, I just tried to stay consistent and target her backhand,” Ruthven said after beating Sokolova. Last year, Ruthven lost in three sets to Sokolova and in two sets to Zuber. Playing with consistency Ruthven got the better of them this time around. “This helps with my confidence and keeping a constant energy. I want to stay confident with my aggressiveness on the court,” Ruthven said. The clinching match on Wednesday against the Dons came from senior captain Faith Chin at No. 2 singles. She’s now entering her third year as a varsity starter. “Her backhand was a lot weaker than her forehand, so I just kept hitting to it until opening up to her forehand, and she couldn’t keep up with it. articles.text: Piedmont looks to regroup after a disappointing loss to Napa in the season opener. It was a rough start to the season for Piedmont High’s football team, losing 28-7 to Napa at Witter Field on Friday, August 28. PHS scored the game’s final touchdown with 8:39 left in the fourth quarter. “Our youth showed up at the worst time. But it’s a lesson; we’re a young team and didn’t have our best week of practice. It’s all about how we push each other in practice,” coach Jordan Seiden said. “Finishing” will be the word of the week for Seiden as Piedmont looks ahead toward hosting St. Mary’s on Friday, September 4. PHS had chances to capitalize in short-yardage situations, but struggled to get the ball across the line or hold off Napa on the defensive side. They got down to the two-yard line after a big catch and run by Rehan Mumtaz midway through the first quarter, but failed to score. In the second quarter, a fumbled snap on 3rd-and-1 led to a turnover on downs. They got to the Napa 29 early in the third quarter, but the drive stalled after that. Defensively, PHS couldn’t stop the run as Napa gained 314 of its yards on the ground. Napa gashed Piedmont with a 60-yard touchdown in the first quarter, and a 30-yard touchdown in the final seconds of the second quarter in a 4th-and-3 situation. They also converted two fourth downs on their way to their fourth score. “We’ve got to finish. It’s a part of being young and not understanding the importance of an inch in a game of inches. The message is to finish and they are going to get tired of hearing that word. We got down the field multiple times and only came away with one touchdown,” Seiden said. The St. Mary’s Panthers are coming off a 41-6 loss to Diablo Valley and finished 1-9 last season, perhaps giving the Highlanders a chance to get back on track. Game Recap Napa struck first on a fiveplay, 61 yard drive that capped off with a six-yard touchdown carry. On Piedmont’s ensuing drive, Mumtaz broke a 32 yard run on a screen down to the two-yard line, but things died after that. Staff Photos A loss of five yards on 1st-andGoal led to a false start on second down. A three-yard loss made things bleaker before quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster ran to the 10. An incompletion on fourth down turned it over with 6:07 left, leading to a four-play drive that resulted in a 60-yard touchdown run after nearly two minutes— making it 14-0. PHS drove to the Napa 47 on its next possession, but two sacks resulted in a punt on 4th-and-20. At the end of the second quarter, Napa scored on a 30-yard carry as time expired on an end-around in a 4th-and-3 situation. In the third, Piedmont started the quarter by driving 31 yards to the Napa 29, but three incompletions ended things. Napa scored its final touchdown with 10:30 left in the fourth quarter on a 12-play, 45 yard drive that featured two fourth-down conversions. John Bunje recovered a fumble with 8:52 left at the Napa 12 to help out the offense. Cyrus Emanuelson completed a pass to Owen Curran down to the one, leading to Colby Hong punching the ball into the end zone. Final stats: Cha-Foster had 128 passing yards. Emanuelson had 57 passing yards, completing five of six passes. George Saunders had five receptions for 123 yards. Mumtaz had three receptions for 47 yards, to go along with 24 rushing yards. Bunje had a fumble recovery, Curran had a pass defense. articles.text: The Piedmont Highlanders JV football team suffered a loss in their season opener to the Napa Grizzlies, falling 22-6 on Friday, August 28. Piedmont’s offensive line gave quarterbacks Ernie Hildreth and Gio López strong protection throughout the game, allowing both quarterbacks to finish without any interceptions. The Highlanders were led by team captains, Ernie Hildreth (1), Alex Perez (69), Lev Kuluva (18), and Gio López (25) On the opening kickoff, Gael Fierro sent the ball deep, and Lev Kuluva (18) burst downfield through Napa’s blockers to the 17-yard line, forcing Napa to begin its first drive 83 yards from the end zone. Throughout most of the first half, Piedmont’s defense kept Napa off the scoreboard. Piedmont right tackle Ozem Fitzgerald came up with a huge fourthdown quarterback sack in the red zone, while captain Ernie Hildreth relayed defensive calls from Coach Assadi and helped lead the Highlanders to several key stops. With just two seconds remaining in the half, Napa connected on a controversial touchdown pass near the edge of the end zone. The play left Piedmont players and spectators questioning if the receiver had reached the end zone, but the touchdown stood, giving Napa an 8-0 lead heading into halftime. Coming out of halftime, Piedmont’s Will Dietrick returned the opening kickoff 17 yards, setting up the Highlanders’ offense at their own 40-yard line. Despite battling an injury suffered earlier in the game, Dietrick continued to fight through the pain and contribute for the Highlanders. The Grizzlies forced a turnover on Piedmont’s next possession, but the Highlanders’ defense made them work for every yard. Despite several key stops, Napa eventually broke through for a touchdown to extend its lead. Another kick return late in the third by Will Dietrick gave the Highlanders possession at their own 23-yard line. Despite the long field ahead, quarterback Gio López handed the ball off several times to running back Joseph Logwood, who helped move Piedmont downfield and into field position at Napa’s 38-yard line. Quarterback Gio López then fired a deep pass to Lev Kuluva, who made a diving 14-yard reception to carry the Highlanders’ momentum to Napa’s 24-yard line. Keeping the momentum alive, López dropped another dime, this time lofting a fade to Gael Fierro, who rose above the defender and caught a 24-yard touchdown pass to put the Highlanders on the board for the first time. Although the Highlanders failed on a 2-point conversion attempt, they were still in the game. With hope still alive, the Highlanders attempted to win the ball back and mount one final scoring drive. However, Napa regained possession and added one final touchdown at the end of the game, sealing the 22-6 loss for Piedmont. Key players include Gio López, who helped lead the Highlanders’ offense and threw Piedmont’s lone touchdown pass, and Gael Fierro, who led the team in receptions. Ernie Hildreth and Will Dietrick each recorded eight tackles to lead the defense. Next week Piedmont returns home to face Gunn High School of Palo Alto at 4:00 p.m. at Witter Field. The team looks to bounce back and get its first win of the season. Lev Kuluva (18) Photos by Graham Smith Gio López (25) Gael Fierro (15)

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) opens its 2026-27 season with a theatrical adaptation of Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, bringing the 1959 spy thriller to the Toni Rembe Theater beginning September 22. The production is adapted and directed by Emma Rice. Rice previously directed A.C.T.’s Brief Encounter and Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s The Wild Bride. Rice’s production uses seven performers, live music, movement and theatrical effects to tell the story of Roger Thornhill, an advertising executive who is mistaken for a Cold War spy and forced to flee across the country. The production features a 1950s-inspired soundtrack and a theatrical recreation of the film’s famous Mount Rushmore sequence. The cast includes Danny Collins as Thornhill, Evangeline Dickson as Mrs. Townsend and understudy, Patrycja Kujawska as Eve Kendall and others, Simon Oskarsson as Valerian and others, Katy Owen as the Professor and others, Bryony Pennington as Anna and others, and Karl Queensborough as Phillip Vandamm and others. Sam Archer will take over the role of Valerian and others beginning October 10. “What makes Emma Rice’s North by Northwest so exhilarating is that it isn’t trying to recreate Hitchcock’s film frame for frame,” said Andy Chan Donald, A.C.T.’s artistic producing director and acting artistic director. “Instead, it captures the wit, suspense, and cinematic scale of the original while embracing everything that makes live theater extraordinary.” “The result is a production that honors a beloved classic while becoming something entirely its own — a thrilling reminder that the stage can be every bit as breathtaking as the silver screen,” Donald added. The original North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant and Eva Marie Saint, follows Thornhill as he is pursued across the country after being mistaken for a government agent. Directed by Hitchcock and released in 1959, the film is widely regarded as one of the director’s major works. The show will run at A.C.T.’s Toni Rembe Theater from September 22 through October 18, with press night scheduled for September 23. Post-show conversations are scheduled for Sept. 29, Oct. 4 and Oct. 7. A tasting event is scheduled for Oct. 6, and PlayTime, an interactive theater workshop, will take place before the Oct. 17 matinee. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets. The cast of North By Northwest includes Danny Collins as Thornhill.

Marin Theatre opens its 60th season with the Bay Area premiere of The White Chip, a play about alcoholism and recovery, running now through September 20. Written by Sean Daniels and directed by Marin Theatre Executive Artistic Director Lance Gardner, the play follows Steven, a successful theater director whose career and personal life are increasingly affected by his struggle with alcohol addiction. After his drinking disrupts his relationships and professional life, Steven begins the process of recovery by accepting Alcoholics Anonymous’ white chip, which is given to people marking 24 hours of sobriety or expressing a desire to stop drinking. The play draws on Daniels’ own experiences with addiction and recovery. Gardner, who will mark 20 years of sobriety in 2027, said the production has personal significance for him. “The White Chip isn’t my story, but the decision to produce it is a very personal one,” Gardner said in a press release. “2027 will mark 20 years of sobriety for me. Making the choice to abstain from drugs and alcohol opened the doors that led me to the helm of Marin Theatre and probably saved my life.” Gardner said the play addresses the stigma surrounding addiction and recovery through its combination of comedy and drama. “The White Chip confronts the stigma of addiction and recovery head on with a hilarious and heart wrenching story which has the power to enlighten and inspire audiences whether or not they’ve experienced this kind of thing firsthand,” he said. The White Chip premiered at Merrimack Repertory Theatre before productions at New York’s 59E59 Theater and MCC Theater. It has since been produced by theaters around the country. Benjamin Clark will make his Marin Theatre debut as Steven. His regional theater credits include Asolo Repertory Theatre, Barrington Stage Company, Round House Theatre, Olney Theatre Center and Everyman Theatre. Danny Scheie and Lyndsy Kail round out the cast, portraying people in Steven’s life. Scheie previously appeared at Marin Theatre in The Cherry Orchard and Lady in the Dark and directed the theater’s productions of Splittin’ the Raft and The Pavilion. Kail has performed with California Shakespeare Theater, Center Repertory Company and San Jose Stage Company, among others. The White Chip will be performed at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. in Mill Valley. articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden’s outdoor summer concert series Sunset Sessions continues Thursday, September 17 with a performance by The Real John Gary. articles.text: The Flower Piano festival will return to the San Francisco Botanical Garden September 10 through 20, bringing live performances and public piano installations to the 55-acre garden. The annual event features 12 grand and baby grand pianos placed throughout the garden, where visitors can attend scheduled performances, watch community groups perform or play the instruments during designated open play sessions. Flower Piano was created in 2017 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Fortissimo and Dean Mermell in collaboration with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The festival has since become an annual event at the botanical garden. This year’s lineup includes daily performances by La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9, and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, whose repertoire blends hip-hop, jazz and classical music. The San Francisco Ballet School is also scheduled to perform in this year’s festival. The school’s performances will give audiences an opportunity to see ballet students perform in an outdoor setting as part of a festival that combines music and community programming. The 2026 festival also includes an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, featuring seating, food and beverages, and evening performances. During open play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels to use. Attendees are encouraged to bring picnic blankets as seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and tickets, is available at https://gggp.org/flowerpiano. The beloved Flower Piano festival returns to Golden Gate Park this month.

articles.text: Inspiration is elusive, to say the least. So, seeking wisdom, I asked my 11-year-old granddaughter to enlighten me. Miriam offered to write today’s article. “Hold your horses” after I said “I need your thoughts.” She thought a minute, and said that Dolly Parton was an inspiration. While that quality comes in many forms, it should be a positive breath and not a reaction to negativity. In these respects, Dolly Parton was the embodiment of the positive. Any negatives were handled with humor and diplomacy. Well… How about the good things she accomplished? As we all know, she died a few days ago at the age of 80. While rumors of ill health circulated, Dolly presented a positive picture of good health. She even took to social media saying: “I ain’t dead yet.” Despite the cancellation of concerts, she presented her fans a hopeful medical outlook. Miriam knows that I appreciate classical music. Do I like country music? I certainly do, and I am drawn to the older country music songs. Dolly Parton was a “country music star.” This is a small issue because Dolly Parton was a huge success. She had dignity and sincere musicality. How I wish the current crop of classical musicians had these qualities. In life, everyone experiences hurdles, which are necessary in our art. Dolly Parton had more than her share of hurdles to overcome. She experienced poverty and parental illiteracy in the beginning. This situation resulted in autobiographical songs which stress her love for family and beyond. These songs offer advice for life. Her song “Coat of Many Colors” is a perfect example of her underlying philosophy. Dolly Parton performing at the Grand Ole Opry, April 24, 2005. Dolly unified musical genius and human universality in music and in life.

The Trefethen story began in 1968, when Eugene and Catherine Trefethen purchased a neglected property just north of the town of Napa. articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is watching one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers movies in a comfortable setting with lively discussion afterwards. September’s film, Monsieur Ibrahim Et Les Fleurs Du Coran, is a touching and heartwarming French film from 2003, directed by François Dupeyron. It tells the story of a friendship between a Jewish teenager named Momo, played by Pierre Boulanger, and a Turkish Muslim grocer, Monsieur Ibrahim, played by Omar Sharif. The film is set in a working-class neighborhood in 1960s Paris. Momo lives with his lawyer father, who struggles with severe depression, and cannot meet Momo’s emotional needs after his mother leaves them. Momo, their meal provider, faces a tight household budget, and resorts to occasional thefts from Monsieur Ibrahim, the local ‘Arab’ grocer. Despite noticing these thefts, Monsieur Ibrahim decides to support Momo by encouraging a gradual increase in their friendship. Through their daily shop interactions, Momo finds solace and a sense of security with his newfound connection to the grocer whose wisdom, consistent patience and thoughtful observation creates a stable, non-judgmental environment, a stark contrast to Momo’s cold and hostile home life. A pivotal moment in the film occurs when Momo’s father abandons him, leaving behind only a short note and a small sum of money on the kitchen table. Momo, while keeping his father’s absence a secret from Monsieur Ibrahim, deepens his connection with the grocer by sharing experiences and learning from his new friend’s unique interpretation of the Koran. Eventually, Monsieur Ibrahim learns of Momo’s father’s abandonment, and seizes the opportunity to broaden Momo’s understanding of the world by impulsively buying a car, and inviting Momo to embark on a road trip to Turkey to visit his hometown. Momo’s encounter with a Sufi troupe performing the whirling dervishes dance helps him mature and embrace a broader understanding of a different culture. Later, as their car approaches Monsieur Ibrahim’s town, he asks Momo to get out so he can enter his birthplace alone for the first time in many years. The film then unfolds showing how Momo later accepts a new life back in his Paris neighborhood as the inheritor of his friend’s legacy. Director François Dupeyron skillfully evoked nostalgia in this film. With a delicate yet never sentimental touch, he introduces us to two individuals from vastly different ages and backgrounds in an engaging and insightful manner. Pierre Boulanger and Omar Sharif, the two stars, complement each other perfectly, making for an enjoyable viewing experience as we watch them work together. Monsieur Ibrahim will be shown on Thursday, September 10 at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The movie is free to anyone 18 and over. Our next movie is The Grand Budapest Hotel, a 2014 comedy/drama, to be shown on October 8 at 1 p.m.

Begin on a leash if you have to, creating gentle tension to discourage moving forward, and always place your dog back in the same spot if they get up. Practice at longer distances as your pup gets better, and gradually introduce distractions, such as dropped food. A reliable stay gives you those precious extra seconds to frame the perfect shot. Teaching your pooch to “chin prop” takes your photos to the next level. Using a treat, lure your pup’s nose down until their chin is braced on the desired place, such as the arm of the couch or a fun prop. articles.text: This summer Piedmont Scouts in Troop 4 completed an exciting backpacking trip through the Sierra Nevada mountains. Over the course of seven days, 54 miles and 10,500 feet of elevation gain, the trek took us through numerous lakes and mountain passes in the Ansel Adams and Yosemite Wildernesses. Every day brought new scenery, from dense forests and open mountain meadows to towering granite peaks and clear alpine lakes. Some of the most memorable views came when we reached a high point on the trail and could look back over the valleys and lakes we had hiked past. Each day began with breakfast before we packed up and left camp around 10 a.m. We would hike for several miles, stopping for lunch along the trail before continuing toward our next campsite. Although carrying a backpack for miles and climbing steep mountain passes can be tiring, the scenery made the effort worthwhile. Reaching the top of a pass was especially rewarding, since it felt like the hardest part had been completed (even though the downhill was usually just as hard). Since most Scouts on the trip were sleeping in hammocks, we rigged tarps over them whenever it looked like it might rain. On one occasion, the rain actually began, accompanied by hail, putting our setups to the test. Fortunately, everyone stayed dry until the storm passed, thanks to our scouting skills. At camp, there was plenty to do besides setting up and cooking dinner. We swam in the cold mountain lakes, played Prepared for rain at Vandenburg Lake cards, talked with each other, and relaxed in our hammocks after an eventful day on the long trails. Our route took us through high mountain terrain, with many campsites at altitudes above 9,000 feet and four mountain passes, with the highest, Red Peak Pass, reaching over 11,200 feet. Our route started at Isberg Trailhead in Sierra National Forest, and led us through two miles of burned out forest to the beginning of Ansel Adams Wilderness. We stayed at Cora Lake that night and on the second day hiked 10 miles over Isberg Pass into Yosemite National Park. We followed that day with another grueling 10 miles up and over Red Peak Pass to Ottoway Lake where we finally gave ourselves a break. The elevation made hiking more difficult, especially on the steep climbs, but it also gave us some of the best views of the trip. With the proliferation of automobiles after World War II, electric streetcars were no longer considered efficient. Buses, later run by AC Transit District, took over the streetcar routes. Homeowners along the train’s route came out to wave goodbye, as the motorman saluted back. articles.text: Happy September, all! THE PIEDMONT PREMIUM While external economic headlines fluctuate, Piedmont’s real estate market continues to operate in a strategic league of its own. This enduring desirability has long rested on what makes Piedmont special: top-ranking public schools, hyper-responsive city services, and an unmatched quality of life. Yet, the current momentum is being amplified by an exceptionally well-capitalized class of buyers. Equipped with substantial liquidity and the ability to close quickly with cash, these buyers are moving with remarkable speed. The result is a market operating at peak performance. Today, virtually every well-presented listing is met with immediate, intense demand, routinely commanding multiple competitive offers within days of hitting the market. For homeowners, this alignment of scarcity and affluent demand ensures Piedmont remains an absolute stronghold for sellers. MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: If you own a condo, there were some important changes to condo financing rules this August that are worth knowing about. Since the tragic condo collapse in Surfside, Florida in 2021, lenders have paid much closer attention to the safety, finances, insurance, and deferred maintenance of condo buildings. That has made financing difficult in some projects that were previously easy to lend on. The new rules create two very different paths. Condo projects with 10 units or fewer now have a much simpler approval process, while projects with 11 or more units face a more detailed review than ever before. For owners in larger buildings, issues with insurance, building finances, major repairs, or litigation could limit the financing available to future buyers or make refinancing more difficult. If you own or are considering buying a condo, understanding whether the project itself qualifies for financing has become just as important as whether you qualify for a mortgage.
